title: not "suffering"
hookLine: not "suffering" — the wobble in the wheel; the itch under everything

cards: You finally get the thing. The new phone, the weekend off, the apartment with the good light. And for a day or two it's wonderful.
Then, very quietly, something starts to itch. The phone has a scratch. The weekend is already half over on Saturday night.
The light is great, but the neighbors are loud. Nothing is wrong, exactly. It just doesn't quite sit right.
There's a word for that. It's usually translated as suffering, which is why so many people think Buddhism is gloomy. But the word is smaller and stranger than suffering.

teach.b: Dukkha. It's the first big word of the Buddha's teaching, and it's almost impossible to translate. Suffering is the usual choice.
Some translators say stress, or unsatisfactoriness, which is accurate and nobody can say it twice. So teachers often reach for a picture instead. A popular explanation splits the word in two.

teach.h: DU, BAD. KHA, THE AXLE HOLE.
teach.b: Kha, a hole, and in particular the hole in the middle of a wheel, where the axle goes. A cart with a badly fitted wheel still rolls. You still get where you're going.
But every turn has a little jolt in it. That's dukkha. Its opposite is sukha, a good axle hole, which came to mean happiness: a smooth ride.
Scholars aren't sure that's where the word really comes from. But the picture has stuck because it fits. Buddhist teachers describe three layers of it.
The first is plain pain: a toothache, a breakup, a funeral. Nobody needs that explained.
The second is the pain of change: the good thing that's already ending while you're enjoying it, the Sunday evening feeling.

The third is the subtlest: the low hum of everything being conditioned, dependent, never quite solid enough to rest on. The itch under everything. Seeing the wobble clearly is not the same as being crushed by it.

how: Buddhists learn dukkha as the first of the four noble truths, and many teachers invite students simply to recognize it in daily life, the aches, the endings, the restlessness, without adding blame or panic.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: the hole where the axle goes

s: it covers plain pain, but also the pain of change and a quieter itch under everything.
dukkha's opposite, sukha, came to mean happiness
a well-fitted axle hole: a smooth ride.
the Buddha taught dukkha to make people gloomy
he named it so it could be understood, the first step toward the end of it.

games.q: it's a perfect Sunday afternoon. then you notice you're already sad that tomorrow is Monday. which layer of dukkha is that?
games.why: the pain of change: the good thing that's already ending while you're still in it. teachers name it as the second layer.

practice: Today the bell gives you a little longer: about forty-five seconds. Notice one small wobble right now. A tight shoulder.
A worry about later. A message you haven't answered. Don't fix it.
Just name it: this too. Then notice that the wobble and the breath are both here, and the breath is still coming in and going out. Stay with both until the bell.

wordCard.voice: Dukkha. Not only suffering: the wobble in the wheel, the itch under things, the ride that's never perfectly smooth. Eighth word.

orig.note: Pali: the unsatisfactoriness of things. Sanskrit duḥkha; its opposite is sukha.

carryVoice: Your line: this too. Two small words for the small wobbles, and the big ones. Day eight.

sources.ref: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11): dukkha as the first noble truth
Dukkhata Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 45.165): the three kinds of dukkha
